92.title: The letter of victory
92.hook: from the wilderness the Guru writes to the emperor Aurangzeb in Persian, rebuking broken oaths
92.tomorrow: Nanded, 1708: the Guru is the Granth
92.howItsDone: The Zafarnama is kept in the Dasam Granth, and Sikhs read and recite it, often in the original Persian, especially when remembering the events of 1704 to 1706.

screen: `DAY NINETY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chali Mukte, the forty who left and came back, and the paper the Guru tore up. Your line was you can always come back. Did you hold a door open for someone? Day ninety-two.
screen: `CHALI MUKTE — YOU CAN ALWAYS COME BACK.`

segments.voice: There's the letter written in fury, and the letter that actually gets sent: shorter, and harder to argue with. Here is a man who has lost almost everything. His city is gone. His mother is gone. All four of his sons are gone, two in battle and two behind a wall. He's in a small village in the dry country of Punjab, with a handful of followers. And he picks up a pen and writes to the emperor himself, Aurangzeb. He calls it a letter of victory.
screen: `THE LETTER THAT GETS SENT.` → `EVERYTHING LOST.` → `A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Zafarnama. Zafar is victory, nama is a letter, or a book. The letter of victory. Guru Gobind Singh wrote it in Persian, the language of the Mughal court, in verse: a little over a hundred couplets. Tradition says two Sikhs, Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh, carried it all the way south to the emperor's camp in the Deccan. It opens the way a letter to a king would, with praise, but the praise isn't for the king. It's for God. Then it turns to the emperor, and it doesn't flatter. At Anandpur, the letter says, your commanders swore oaths, on the Qur'an itself, that the Guru and his people could leave in safety. And the moment they left, they were attacked. The Guru writes as someone who takes an oath seriously, and holds the emperor to his own faith's promise. One couplet Sikhs often quote says, in paraphrase, that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Sikhs read it carefully: not a love of fighting, but a last resort, after every other door is shut. So why victory? The Guru had no army to speak of and no home. The victory is in the telling. Truth, said plainly, to the face of power, by a man with nothing left to lose. Tradition says the emperor was shaken by it, and that he died not long after, in 1707. Historians aren't sure he ever read it. Sikhs keep it in the Dasam Granth, the collection of writings linked to the tenth Guru, and still read it aloud.
screen: `ZAFARNAMA — THE LETTER OF VICTORY.` · `IN PERSIAN, TO THE EMPEROR.` · `YOU SWORE ON THE QUR'AN, AND BROKE IT.` · `THE SWORD ONLY WHEN ALL ELSE FAILS.` · then, large: `VICTORY IS THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly for a moment. Think of something true you haven't said. Maybe to someone who let you down. Maybe to someone you let down. Maybe just to yourself. Now find one sentence for it. Not the angry draft. The short one. Clear, honest, without cruelty. If you have paper, write it down. If not, say it once, silently. You don't have to send it. Just let it be true, and let it be yours. The bell holds the time.
Zafarnama. The letter of victory, written in Persian by Guru Gobind Singh to the emperor Aurangzeb, holding him to his broken oaths.
screen: `ZAFARNAMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: victory is the truth. Today, write one honest sentence, and cut every word from it that's there to hurt. Day ninety-two.

93.title: Nanded, 1708: the Guru is the Granth
93.hook: before he dies the Guru tells the Sikhs that the scripture is now their Guru
93.carry: the book is the guru now
93.howItsDone: In every gurdwara the Guru Granth Sahib is installed each morning on a raised throne under a canopy and put to rest at night, and a daily hukamnama, a line chosen by opening it at random, is read out as the Guru's word for the day.

screen: `DAY NINETY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zafarnama, the letter of victory, sent to an emperor. Your line was victory is the truth. Did you find your one honest sentence? Day ninety-three.
screen: `ZAFARNAMA — VICTORY IS THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: When the one who holds a family together is gone, who decides? Who do we go to? Few people like asking it out loud. From Guru Nanak on, the Sikhs had an answer: the next Guru. Nanak chose Angad. Angad chose Amar Das. Nine times the light was handed on, person to person. Now it's 1708. Guru Gobind Singh is far from Punjab, in the south of India, at a town called Nanded on the Godavari river. He is wounded, and he knows he is dying. His four sons are gone. Everyone around him is waiting for the name. And the answer he gives is not a person.
screen: `WHO DO WE GO TO NOW?` → `NINE TIMES, PERSON TO PERSON.` → `NANDED, 1708.`

segments.voice: Guru Granth Sahib. Guru, often explained as the one who leads from darkness to light. Granth, a book, a volume. Sahib, a word of respect, like lord or master. Here's what happened, as Sikhs tell it. At Nanded, an assassin stabbed the Guru. The wound was stitched, and then it tore open again. Before he died, in October 1708, he gathered the Sikhs, and he bowed before the scripture: the Adi Granth that Guru Arjan had compiled, the one you met on day sixty-two, with the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur now added. And he told them that after him there would be no more human Gurus. The Word in this book was their Guru. The authority of the community, the Khalsa gathered together, would stand alongside it. Sikhs call these two the Guru Granth and the Guru Panth. That is a bold step. Nobody could inherit it, buy it, or fight over it. The Guru is now the same for everyone, and it speaks in the hymns of the Gurus and of saints from other backgrounds too. That's why a gurdwara looks the way it does. The Granth sits on a raised throne, under a canopy. Someone waves a whisk over it, the way you would for a king. In many gurdwaras, at night it's carried to its own room to rest, and brought out again at dawn. It isn't treated like a book on a shelf. It's treated the way you'd treat a living teacher, because that's what Sikhs say it is. And after every Ardas, many congregations sing a couplet that says it plainly: all Sikhs are commanded to accept the Granth as the Guru.
screen: `A WOUND THAT TEARS OPEN.` · `NO MORE HUMAN GURUS.` · `THE GRANTH AND THE PANTH.` · `TREATED AS A LIVING TEACHER.` · then, large: `THE BOOK IS THE GURU NOW.`

segments.voice: If you have a gutka, a small prayer book, or the Guru Granth Sahib itself, open it now. If you don't, open a page of it online, or just picture one: the wide page, the Gurmukhi script. Don't try to read it all. Let your eyes rest on one line. If you can understand it, stay with its meaning. If you can't, stay with its shape. Sikhs say this is how the Guru still speaks: one line, to one person, today. The bell holds the time.
Guru Granth Sahib. The Sikh scripture, which Guru Gobind Singh named as the Guru after him. The tenth Guru was the last human one.
screen: `GURU GRANTH SAHIB — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the book is the guru now. Today, open the Granth, or a page of it, and read one line slowly, as if it were said to you. Day ninety-three.

94.title: Water for the enemy
94.hook: in battle, Bhai Kanhaiya gave water to wounded soldiers of both sides, and the Guru told him to add ointment too
94.tomorrow: the needle for the next world
94.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Kanhaiya as a model of seva for everyone, and many Sikh relief groups today serve people in disasters and conflicts regardless of who they are.

screen: `DAY NINETY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanded, and the Guru Granth Sahib named as the Guru for all time. Your line was the book is the guru now. Did one line from it find you? Day ninety-four.
screen: `GURU GRANTH SAHIB — THE BOOK IS THE GURU NOW.`

segments.voice: The ten Gurus' stories are told. For two days now, short ones about the people around them. Start with a question. Who is the person you argue with most? Online, at work, at the holiday table. Suppose that person were hurt, on the ground, asking for water, with your own side watching to see what you'd do. That's where today's story happens, on a battlefield near Anandpur, in the years of the sieges. Smoke, noise, men down on both sides. And one Sikh walking through it all with a leather water bag on his back, kneeling, pouring, moving on. His name was Bhai Kanhaiya. And his own side was furious with him.
screen: `THE ONE YOU ARGUE WITH MOST.` → `HURT, AND ASKING FOR WATER.` → `A WATER BAG ON THE BATTLEFIELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as Sikhs tell it. Bhai Kanhaiya's seva during the fighting was carrying water to the wounded. But he didn't check uniforms. He gave water to the Sikhs who were hurt, and he gave water to the soldiers attacking them, exactly the same. Some Sikhs saw it and went to Guru Gobind Singh. He's helping the enemy, they said. The men he revives will fight us again tomorrow. So the Guru called him in and asked him, is it true? And Bhai Kanhaiya said yes. Then he gave the answer Sikhs have repeated ever since. On that field, he said, I don't see Sikhs and I don't see enemies. In every face I see only you, my Guru. The Guru didn't scold him. He was pleased. And he handed him a box of balm, an ointment for wounds, and said: from now on, don't just give water. Dress their wounds too. Think about what the Guru did there. He didn't just allow it. He made it bigger. The Guru Granth Sahib has a line that Sikhs connect to this story, where Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase, that no one is his enemy and no one a stranger; he gets along with everyone. Tradition says Bhai Kanhaiya went on to found a community of Sikhs devoted to this kind of service, the Sevapanthis, and they still exist. When Sikhs tell the story today, they come back to the water bag.
screen: `WATER FOR BOTH SIDES.` · `HE'S HELPING THE ENEMY.` · `IN EVERY FACE I SEE YOU.` · `NOW DRESS THEIR WOUNDS TOO.` · then, large: `EVERY FACE IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and breathe. Bring back the person you argue with. Picture their face, not their opinions. Their tired eyes. The way they look when they're worried. Now picture yourself handing them a glass of water. Nothing else. No debate. Just the glass. Notice what happens in your chest when you do. Resistance is fine; that's honest. Then, if you can, try to see what Bhai Kanhaiya said he saw in every face. The bell holds the time.
Water for the enemy. Bhai Kanhaiya's seva: water for the wounded on both sides, and, at the Guru's word, balm for their wounds too.
screen: `WATER FOR THE ENEMY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: every face is his. Today, do one real kindness for someone you disagree with, and don't mention the disagreement. Day ninety-four.

screen: `DAY 94 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE NEEDLE FOR THE NEXT WORLD.`

95.title: The needle for the next world
95.word: The needle for the next world
95.hook: tradition says Nanak gave rich Duni Chand a needle to return to him in the next world, and Duni Chand understood
95.tomorrow: Camp 2 close: one light, ten lamps
95.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Duni Chand's needle to children and in talks at the gurdwara as a reminder that wealth stays behind, while remembrance, honest work and sharing go with a person.

screen: `DAY NINETY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Kanhaiya, carrying water for the enemy. Your line was every face is his. Did you manage a kindness for someone you disagree with? Day ninety-five.
screen: `WATER FOR THE ENEMY — EVERY FACE IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Some people put their success on display. The car in the driveway. The watch that catches the light. The photos from the trip. In old Lahore, the story goes, there was a rich man named Duni Chand who had a simpler system. On the roof of his house flew a row of flags, one flag for every hundred thousand rupees he owned. The more flags, the richer he was, and the whole street could count them. One day Guru Nanak came to town, and Duni Chand invited him in, proud to host a holy man. And before he left, Nanak gave his rich host a gift. It was a needle.
screen: `THE CAR, THE WATCH, THE PHOTOS.` → `A FLAG FOR EVERY FORTUNE.` → `NANAK'S GIFT: A NEEDLE.`

segments.voice: This is one of the old janamsakhi stories, the life stories of Nanak that Sikhs have told for centuries. Nanak handed Duni Chand the needle and asked a favor. Keep this safe for me, he said. And when we meet in the next world, give it back. Duni Chand, eager to please, said of course. He took the needle to his wife and told her about the honor. She looked at him for a long moment. And how exactly, she asked, are you going to take a needle with you when you die? That landed. Duni Chand went straight back to Nanak. I can't do it, he said. Nothing goes with me. Not a needle. Not the flags. Then Nanak asked him, gently, the real question. If you can't take a needle, what will you take? The story says Duni Chand understood, and began to share what he had, giving it away to the hungry. Notice how Nanak teaches here. He doesn't lecture a rich man about money. He hands him one tiny object and lets him discover the rest, with a little help from his wife. Guru Nanak says the same thing plainly in the Guru Granth Sahib. Writing of wealth, he says, in paraphrase, that many have been ruined for its sake, and that it does not go with anyone who dies. What does go? Sikhs answer with the Name remembered, the honest work done, and what was shared. The flags stay on the roof.
screen: `KEEP IT, AND GIVE IT BACK LATER.` · `HOW WILL YOU TAKE A NEEDLE?` · `NOTHING GOES WITH ME.` · `THE NAME, THE WORK, THE SHARING.` · then, large: `WHAT GOES WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Look around you and pick one thing you own. Your phone, a ring, a mug, a jacket. Hold it or just look at it. Think about how you got it. What it cost. How much it matters to you. Now picture Duni Chand's wife asking you her question: and how will you take this with you? No guilt needed. Just let the question sit next to the thing. Then think of one thing in your life that could go with you. The bell holds the time.
The needle for the next world. Nanak's gift to Duni Chand, a tiny object with a big question inside it: what goes with you?
screen: `THE NEEDLE FOR THE NEXT WORLD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what goes with you. Today, when you're tempted to buy or keep something, ask the needle's question once. Then share one thing. Day ninety-five.

96.title: Camp 2 close: one light, ten lamps
96.hook: Sikhs speak of one light passing through all ten Gurus, and now resting in the Granth and the Khalsa
96.howItsDone: Sikhs honor the ten Gurus as one light in ten forms, and mark each Guru's birth and passing with gurpurabs; when speaking of a Guru's death they often say he merged into the divine light.

screen: `DAY NINETY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the needle for the next world, and Duni Chand's flags. Your line was what goes with you. Did the needle's question stop you once? Day ninety-six.
screen: `THE NEEDLE — WHAT GOES WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: At a candlelight vigil, one person lights a candle, then tips it toward the next person's wick. That one lights the next, and the next, down the whole line, until the dark street is full of small flames. Watch closely and there's something strange. The first flame never gets smaller. Nothing is taken from it. The light just keeps going. For seventy-five days you've walked through the Sikh story, from a boy born at Talwandi to a Guru bowing before a book at Nanded. Ten Gurus. Sikhs have one word for what connects them all, and it's the word for that flame.
screen: `ONE CANDLE LIGHTS THE NEXT.` → `THE FIRST FLAME NEVER SHRINKS.` → `TEN GURUS, ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: Jot. Light, flame, the light of the divine. Sikhs say there were ten Gurus in body, but one light. It's in the Guru Granth Sahib itself. Two musicians at Guru Arjan's court, Satta and Balwand, sang that the light was the same and the way was the same; only the body changed. Nanak's light in Angad, then in Amar Das, then Ram Das, all the way to Gobind Singh. When a Guru died, Sikhs didn't say he was gone. They said his light merged back into the light. And at Nanded the light didn't go out. It came to rest in two places: the Guru Granth Sahib, and the Khalsa, the community gathered. Look back at what that light did in this camp. Sacha sauda, the true bargain of feeding the hungry. Mardana's rebab, the travels, Kartarpur. Angad's ang, the wrestling ground, the baoli at Goindwal. The Anand, Amritsar, the four rounds of the lavan. Harmandir Sahib, the Adi Granth, Guru Arjan's martyrdom. Miri piri and the Akal Takht. A child Guru, a Guru who gave his head in Chandni Chowk. Vaisakhi, the Panj Pyare, amrit, the Khalsa. The Sahibzade, the Chali Mukte, the Zafarnama. Ten lamps, and the same flame in every one. And the Gurus say that flame isn't only in them. In the evening prayer, Kirtan Sohila, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that in everyone there is a light, and that light is the One. The stories are told. Now the next camp turns to what the light asks you to do with your hands.
screen: `JOT — LIGHT, FLAME.` · `ONLY THE BODY CHANGED.` · `RESTING IN THE GRANTH AND THE KHALSA.` · `A LIGHT IN EVERYONE.` · then, large: `ONE LIGHT, TEN LAMPS.`

segments.voice: If you can, light a lamp or a candle, somewhere safe. If you can't, look at any small light near you, or picture one. Watch the flame. It's never still, and never quite the same shape twice, and yet it's the same flame. Breathe slowly and let your eyes rest there. Think of one person whose light reached you: a parent, a teacher, a friend. Their flame lit yours, and it didn't get smaller. The bell holds the time.
Jot. The divine light, one flame through all ten Gurus, now resting in the Granth and the Khalsa. Camp two is complete.
screen: `JOT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one light, ten lamps. Today, notice one light in someone else, and tell them. Tomorrow, camp three: the practices, starting with seva. Day ninety-six.

97.title: Service without an audience
97.hook: seva is service done with no reward in mind, and it is meant to change the one who serves
97.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, Sikhs of every background do seva side by side, cooking, cleaning and serving, and many try to do it quietly, without asking for thanks or recognition.

screen: `DAY NINETY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, camp two closed with jot, the one light in all ten Gurus. Your line was one light, ten lamps. Did you tell someone about the light you saw in them? Day ninety-seven.
screen: `JOT — ONE LIGHT, TEN LAMPS.`

segments.voice: Welcome to camp three. For seventy-five days you heard the stories. Now, for the next stretch of the path, you try the practices, one at a time, starting with the one Sikhs put first. Here's a small test. The last time you did something good for someone, did you tell anyone? A post, a mention at dinner, a little hint so they'd know it was you? That pull is human. A kindness can feel half finished until someone sees it. Now, a snowy street at six in the morning. One neighbor's walk is already shoveled. Nobody saw who did it. Nobody ever will. That's today's word.
screen: `CAMP THREE: THE PRACTICES.` → `DID YOU TELL ANYONE?` → `THE WALK SHOVELED AT SIX.`

segments.voice: Nishkam seva. Seva you already know from day one: service. Nishkam means without desire. Nish, without; kam, wanting. Service with nothing wanted back. No thanks, no credit, no reward, not even the good feeling of being seen as a good person. The Gurus put it at the heart of Sikh life. In the Sukhmani, the long hymn of peace by Guru Arjan, there's a line on it. In paraphrase, it says that whoever serves without desire for reward reaches the Lord. And Guru Nanak says it from the other side: serve in this world, and you will find a seat in the court of the divine. Here's the surprising part. Seva isn't mainly about the person you help. Of course they matter; the hungry get fed. But the Gurus say seva works on the one who serves. Sikhs say each good thing left unseen starves a little of the self that wants attention. Sikhs call that self haumai, and we'll give it a whole day later this week. So seva is practice, like a scale on a piano. It's how the teaching gets out of your head and into your hands. That's why it opens camp three. In the gurdwara you'll see it everywhere: people chopping onions, wiping tables, washing pots, and nobody announces who they are. A doctor, a student, a grandmother, all with their sleeves rolled up. The rule is simple. Do the good thing. Then walk away.

segments.voice: Settle, and let your breathing slow. Think of one small, unseen kindness you could do today. Refilling the coffee filter at work. Taking a neighbor's bin in. Paying a small bill someone won't notice. Picture yourself doing it. Now picture walking away without saying a word. Notice the little itch to be known. You don't have to fight it. Just see it, and smile at it. Then choose your kindness. The bell holds the time.
Nishkam seva. Selfless service: help given with nothing wanted back, which changes the one who gives it.
screen: `NISHKAM SEVA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: no one needs to know. Today, do the unseen kindness you chose, and tell no one, not even tomorrow. Day ninety-seven.

98.title: Start with the shoes
98.hook: in many gurdwaras one honored seva is minding people's shoes
98.howItsDone: Visitors take off their shoes before entering a gurdwara, and volunteers in the joda ghar, the shoe room, look after them, often cleaning them, as a humble and honored seva.

screen: `DAY NINETY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, nishkam seva, service with nothing wanted back. Your line was no one needs to know. Did you manage a kindness nobody saw? Day ninety-eight.
screen: `NISHKAM SEVA — NO ONE NEEDS TO KNOW.`

segments.voice: Start at your own front door. Muddy sneakers. A boot on its side. Somebody's flip-flop that ended up under the mat. Shoes are ordinary things, and a little bit gross. They carry the street into the house. Now go to the entrance of a big gurdwara on a Sunday. Before anyone goes in, they take off their shoes. Pair after pair after pair. And behind a counter by the door, there's a line of volunteers taking every pair, handing back a token, and stacking them on shelves. Some of them are wiping the shoes clean. And some of those volunteers are people you'd never expect to see there.
screen: `THE PILE BY YOUR DOOR.` → `THOUSANDS OF PAIRS.` → `VOLUNTEERS BEHIND THE COUNTER.`

segments.voice: The shoe room at a gurdwara has a name: the joda ghar, the shoe house. And Sikhs count minding it as an honored seva. That can surprise a visitor. Why would the dirtiest job be the honored one? Because of what shoes mean. In the Punjab the Gurus knew, as in many places, feet and shoes were counted the lowest things, the place where caste and pride said you must never put your hands. The Guru Granth Sahib turns that upside down. Again and again the Gurus ask for the dust of the feet of the holy, the humblest place there is. So a person who takes your shoes, and cleans them, is taking the lowest place on purpose. It's nishkam seva, yesterday's word, in its plainest form. Nobody remembers who held their shoes. Here's something else. When the Sikh community's central authority, the Akal Takht, asks someone to make amends for a wrong, the penance can include cleaning shoes and washing dishes at the gurdwara. It has been asked even of powerful politicians. The shoes are a great leveler. You also can't do this seva and stay proud for long. Try handing a stranger their muddy boots with a smile. So the gurdwara begins where you'd least expect: at the door, on the floor, with the shoes. This week ran from a letter to an emperor, through a book made Guru, water for the enemy, a needle and one light, to a rack of shoes by the door. Camp three starts there, at the bottom.
screen: `THE JODA GHAR, THE SHOE HOUSE.` · `THE DUST OF THE FEET OF THE HOLY.` · `A PENANCE FOR THE POWERFUL.` · `THE LOWEST PLACE, ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `START AT THE SHOES.`

segments.voice: If you can, go to the shoes by your door. Kneel down. Pair them up. Straighten them. Wipe off a little mud if you like. Do your own, and then do someone else's. Go slowly. Notice any small feeling that this is beneath you, and let it be there. If you can't get up right now, picture the shoes, and picture your hands tidying them, one pair at a time. The bell holds the time.

Start with the shoes. The joda ghar, where minding strangers' shoes is an honored seva. Your week: the Zafarnama, the Granth as Guru, water for the enemy, the needle, jot, nishkam seva, and the shoes.
screen: `START WITH THE SHOES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: start at the shoes. Today, when a job feels beneath you, do it first, and do it well. Day ninety-eight.
